context: process factory · refiner, dryer, energy plant and continuous press; fire and dust safety critical

brief.intro: New to this project type? An MDF or particleboard plant turns wood into panels. Logs are debarked and chipped; the chips are steamed and ground into fibre in a refiner, mixed with resin, dried in a long flash-dryer tube, formed into a thick mat and squeezed in a hot continuous press that can be fifty metres long. The endless panel is cut, cooled, sanded and sawn to size. Beside the line stands an energy plant that burns bark and dust to make the hot gas and thermal oil the dryer and the press need. It is a heavy process plant inside a building, with a real risk of fire and dust explosion, so spark detection, extinguishing and explosion venting are built into every duct. The press and the energy plant are the long-lead items and the hardest installations.

glossary.plain: medium-density fibreboard — a panel made of wood fibres bonded with resin.
the machine that grinds steamed chips into fibre between rotating discs.
the pipe that carries fibre from the refiner to the dryer; resin is injected into it.
a long duct in which fibre dries in seconds in a stream of hot gas.
a long press with steel belts that heats and compresses the mat into an endless board.
hot oil that carries heat from the energy plant to the press.
sensors in ducts that detect a spark and trigger water sprays before it reaches a filter or silo.
a rotating rack that lets hot boards cool before stacking.

must_get_right: Order the continuous press and the energy plant first; both are made to order and take the longest to deliver and install.
The press foundation is long, heavy and must be exact; the press is assembled on site over weeks under the supplier's supervision.
Fire and explosion protection is not an add-on: spark detection, extinguishing and venting must be complete and tested before any fibre is produced.
The energy plant must be running before the dryer and the press can be commissioned — it leads the start-up sequence.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by plant area along the process line and by discipline, with every long-lead machine tracked from order to factory test, shipping and arrival.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar for construction; equipment installation may run extended shifts under vendor supervision. Commissioning follows the vendor's programme, and hot commissioning runs continuously once started.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Supplier drawings → press, refiner and energy-plant foundations → building → equipment installation by area, with the energy plant and press as the long parallel jobs → thermal oil, power, air → safety systems tested → energy plant fired → first fibre → first board. The critical path runs through the press or the energy plant.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The process technology and vendor are fixed before design starts; vendor drawings for foundations arrive on the agreed dates; permanent power and water are available before cold commissioning; raw material for trial production is on site.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy machines need crane access and often must enter before the cladding or a wall is closed. Vendor supervisors are booked for fixed periods. Clean, dry, powered conditions are required before precision equipment is unpacked.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: late press or energy plant, press-foundation tolerance, fire during commissioning, emission permit conditions, and a long ramp-up to board quality. Contingency is held before first board.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by plant area and discipline; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the installation crews and the vendor supervisors — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
